Imperfection
ĭm-pẽr-fĕk´shŭn
n. (defect; want of completeness; the incompleteness of the believer's holiness in this life)
Latin imperfectio, from in-, not, and perficere, to finish. The theological question is not whether a Christian is imperfect but what he is to do about knowing it.

Biblical Definition

Imperfection is the believer's present condition. Knowledge is partial: “we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1Co 13:9–10). Obedience is partial: “the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do” (Rom 7:19). Speech especially: “in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man” (Jas 3:2). Denial is self-deception: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1Jn 1:8). And the mature man's own account is Paul's: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Php 3:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines imperfection as defect; want of a part or of completeness; failure; fault; and, in morals, moral failing or defect.

expand to see more

IMPERFECTION, n. Defect; fault; the want of perfection; as the imperfections of nature.

2. Failure; deficiency; incompleteness.

IMPERFECT, a. Not perfect; not complete in all its parts; defective.

2. Not fully formed.

Key Scripture

1Co 13:9 — "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part."

Rom 7:19 — "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do."

Jas 3:2 — "For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body."

1Jn 1:8 — "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."

Php 3:12 — "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Imperfection is used as an excuse to stop striving, or denied so that a man cannot admit what everyone can see.

expand to see more

The first misuse turns a diagnosis into a permission. Nobody's perfect is offered as the end of a conversation about a sin, and it functions as an amnesty. But Paul's own statement in Philippians 3:12 does not stop at the admission; the sentence continues — not as though I had already attained, but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus — and the next verses use the language of an athlete straining forward. The knowledge of imperfection in Scripture always produces pursuit, never permission.

The second misuse is perfectionism, and its cruelty is that it forces sincere people to lie. If a believer must claim victory over conscious sin, then either he redefines sin downward until his record clears, or he conceals what he cannot deny, and both destroy the confession by which sin is dealt with. First John 1:8 is written into a letter about walking in the light and is followed immediately by verse 9 — if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us. The admission is the doorway; a doctrine that closes it has closed the way to cleansing in the name of holiness.

James 3:2 aims at the place where imperfection is most visible and least often owned: in many things we offend all, and the test case is the tongue. A man may hold a clean external record for decades and still be undone by what he says in his own house, which is why the epistle spends a chapter on it. The doctrine is finally a hopeful one, because it is stated in the same breath as its terminus — when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away. The imperfection is real, it is not permanent, and it is not the last thing said about the believer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ek merous (G3313), in part; teleios (G5046), perfect, complete, mature; ptaio (G4417), to stumble, offend; dioko (G1377), to pursue, follow after.

Greek ek merous (G3313) — in part; 1 Corinthians 13:9–12.

Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature, perfect; Philippians 3:12, 3:15, James 3:2, Matthew 5:48.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue; Philippians 3:12–14, 1 Timothy 6:11, Hebrews 12:14.

Usage

"“Not as though I had already attained… but I follow after” — the sentence continues."

"“In many things we offend all” — and the test case is the tongue."

"“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” — and verse 9 follows."
